newsitem.title: USA: Forex mart reflects faith in Europe's EMU resolve.
newsitem.headline: Forex mart reflects faith in Europe's EMU resolve.

text.p: A sharp slump in the German mark following French elections on Sunday underscored market faith in Europe's resolve to push ahead with its single currency plan -- even at the expense of a strong euro.
"I think it's clear from the way the market's trading that EMU takes place even if it is a broader EMU and a weaker euro," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"A delay in EMU is being talked about in some quarters but if people really believed there was going to be a delay there would be a stronger mark and not a weaker one."

The mark slumped and the dollar gained following news of a Socialist victory in French parliamentary elections on Sunday -- a clear sign that the strength, and not the existence, of the single currency was being questioned by traders.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, who was named prime minister on Monday, was swept into office by a disaffected French electorate that decisively rejected the austerity policies of President Jacques Chirac's government.

Voters sent a clear message that policies to fight French unemployment, which currently stands just below 13 percent, should take precedence over strict fiscal discipline in the run-up to monetary union.
And though the party of Francois Mitterand and Jacques Delors is unlikely to abandon its support for EMU, the Socialist mandate appears clear.

"The Socialists have made it very clear that they support monetary union and the euro, just not under the terms that were agreed to," said Hillel Waxman, chief foreign exchange dealer at Bank Leumi Trust Co of New York.
"It looks like this will be a case of moving the goalposts in the middle of the game," Waxman said.
Moving the goalposts could also mean increasing the number of players, a move which would have longer-term negative implications for the German mark, dealers said.

The mark has already come under fire as a result of Bonn's push to revalue German gold reserves over Bundesbank objections. And on Monday, mark selling against a host of other currencies, including the French franc, continued.

"Everyone now believes the criteria will be scuttled in some way," said Bob Savage, chief dealer at Lehman Brothers. "That has shifted the market away from marks and toward safe havens, in particular the dollar."

The dollar had pushed to 1.7320 marks by early afternoon in New York on Monday, its highest level in almost a month. The mark also slumped against the Japanese yen, the Swiss franc, the Spanish peseta, the Italian lira and the British pound.
Traders and analysts predicted that in the months to come, more safe-haven buying could result, boosting the greenback to new heights.
"Given the mess that the euro debate is going to create in Europe ... the best place to look is out of town," said Leumi's Waxman. "The dollar will be the prime beneficiary of that."
